cells.tense: Right now you can hold steady and still ask the question that opens the next step.
cells.act: cut through the inertia with one decisive act
cells.ask: Take something you keep weighing and settle it today — one move, no polished version first.
cells.core:
You bear things well, and you don't stop asking.

What's working is this: the weight stays on your shoulders and the question keeps turning until its far side shows. You listen. You check. Curiosity stays open, and the bearing doesn't harden into a wall. Things make sense around you because you're still asking rather than having locked the answers down.

What this balance can feed next is a decision. Pick something you've been carrying and make the move — the quieter cousin of what you'd do if you weren't busy holding everything up. The clarity you get from asking is where the nerve to act lives, and the two can be the same motion. You don't have to finish understanding first. Answer with your feet.

cells.verb: asking your way forward with fresh eyes

cells.tense: You are bracing for questions that haven't even been asked yet.
cells.act: ask the beginner's question about where to go
cells.ask: Ask one plain beginner's question about where this is going, then stand in this stretch of the road as it actually is.
cells.core:
The asking has outrun the bearing.

You're braced for a conversation nobody has started, tracking what might get said before it's said, and your endurance is pouring into a future that hasn't arrived. Curiosity has turned into prep work — you're checking the ground so thoroughly that you've stopped standing on this part of it. The fire that should come from what you've already built gets spent on what could still go wrong, and anyone walking with you feels the difference. Asking has stopped being exploration and started being defense. You're grinding at a test no one handed you.

A beginning question is available instead: what would this look like if it didn't have to be known yet? Hold it open, genuinely, as a question. Then stand where your feet actually are.

cells.tense: You are standing at a door you already walked through, still steadying it.
cells.act: sense what has not happened yet, with wonder
cells.ask: Turn toward the next curve in the road and be curious about it without needing to see past it.
cells.core:
What should have been set down is still being carried.

Your endurance is charged and it's holding what's already finished — a step you've taken, a job you can do in your sleep. You do what's expected and you do it well, and the forward question sits waiting for you to come back around to it. You don't need more stamina; the tank is fine. You need a reason to look forward instead of back, and that reason usually starts as plain interest in what's next.

So let yourself wonder about something that hasn't happened yet. Not a plan, not a decision — just a look down the road with some lightness in it. That's how the next thing gets close enough to ask about.

cells.tense: You are bending under weight right now and calling it the shape of the road.
cells.act: make the fair call about a feeling, yourself
cells.ask: Look at what you're holding that nobody handed you, and decide for yourself whether it stays.
cells.core:
Bearing has gone unsigned.

You've been carrying a stretch of road nobody else seems to know about, and your version has it that this is simply how the road is. The endurance is real. But the one doing it has stopped signing the work. You describe your own effort as terrain — as though what you're hauling had been sitting there rather than something you picked up along the way. From where they stand, you're fine.

The fair judgment is still yours to make, though. Somewhere in what you're bearing sits a weight you took on without being asked. Look at it quietly and decide whether it belongs to you. The road continues either way. What changes is whether you're walking it or dragging it.

attempts.check: The record does not support saying what the person has survived or failed to learn — so Too Little names the posture, never the history. A reader could reasonably say I've got the endurance backwards: in this seat the strain is that bearing has become harder than the asking, so I've written each cell as a cost of holding, not a lack of strength. The asks survive being wrong: each is the partner's own act (a decisive act, a spark started, a look at what's coming, a fair call about a feeling), small enough to try even if my read of the moment is off. The sentence that serves me more than the person is any line that congratulates them for enduring; I've kept those out.
